articles.title: Pentagon Pressured Starlink to Cede Sovereign Geofencing Controls
articles.content: By Erin Banco and Joey Roulette Oct 23, 2026 Add AL-MONITOR on Google FILE PHOTO: An artilleryman of the Special Rifle Police Battalion sets up Starlink satellite internet system near the frontline in Donetsk region — Stringer By Erin Banco and Joey Roulette WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Well before the throttling this month of Ukraine's military access to Elon Musk's satellite communications system, the Biden and Trump administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn its Starlink service on or off in various countries, according to six former senior US officials familiar with the matter. During the presidency of Joe Biden, the requests included switching off the service to prevent Iranian proxy militias in Yemen and Lebanon from using Starlink to communicate, and activating the service to provide internet access inside Iran and in Ukraine to support its military, said four of the former officials. Similarly, President Donald Trump's administration asked Musk, who is CEO of SpaceX, to make the service available in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in 2025 and 2026, in hopes it would bolster internet access and communications for anti-government protesters, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. All of the people spoke on condition of anonymity. The previous US requests about Starlink access are being reported here for the first time. The recent blowup over restrictions to Ukraine's use of SpaceX satellite services has raised questions about the ties between the US government and Musk, whose company owns systems vital to the US military and to US allies. The Biden-era and Trump requests to Musk show a close relationship in which US administrations rely to an unprecedented degree on a private-sector company to help implement foreign policy. The recent limits on Ukraine, despite being a US ally, have also rattled officials in Europe, some of whom argue that Europe must develop its own military satellite communications capabilities because no viable short-term alternative currently exists. STARSHIELD RESTRICTIONS HOBBLE UKRAINE MILITARY Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last week that his country's access to Starshield, the military version of the Starlink system, had been intentionally limited, interfering with the performance of the country’s military drones. He also said the speeds were reduced for Starlink, which Ukraine uses for some military activities including defense against Russian missile attacks. Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. The Trump administration has acknowledged the slowdown but has not said whether it gave the order. The White House, contacted for comment, referred Reuters to Trump's remarks on Friday, when he said he had not spoken with Musk about Starlink access issues for Ukraine and that "if there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out." Halyna Yusypiuk, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said Ukraine's priority is "to have the service restored to normal speed as soon as possible, as the lives of our people depend on it." SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment, although Musk said in a social media post earlier this week: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately (by the president of the United States).” Democratic US Representative Jason Crow called on Friday for clarity about the recent changes to Ukraine's satellite service, saying there are risks to the US dependence on SpaceX. "Unelected billionaires and private corporations should not decide what is in the best interest of America's national security," Crow said. For Ukraine, the Starlink internet service has become the lifeblood of frontline communication between units, who say there is currently no rival to the capabilities of SpaceX's products. Starshield receivers, largely impervious to radio jamming, are used as onboard guidance systems and to provide links to a remote pilot for Ukrainian drones, including deep behind Russian lines inside Ukraine. MUSK'S INFLUENCE RAISES UNCERTAINTY Musk's role as the strong-willed CEO of a company with outsized influence over US national security has at times raised questions over who is making decisions about SpaceX's satellite services. The SpaceX CEO is "supposed to be a business executive, with government contracts, and he's essentially making huge foreign policy decisions," said Armand Musey, president of Summit Ridge Group, a satellite industry consultancy. "He's sufficiently ambiguous of a person that you don't know if his decisions are sort of his personal quirks, or it's because there's an influence elsewhere that's impacting him," Musey said. In previous years, Musk has moved to limit Ukraine’s access to Starlink. In 2022, according to Reuters reporting, Musk ordered SpaceX personnel to cut Starlink coverage in areas Ukraine was trying to retake, a move that surprised White House officials. Musk has said publicly that he refused a 2022 Ukrainian request to activate his satellite network in Crimea's port city of Sevastopol to aid an attack on Russia's fleet there, saying he feared complicity in a major act of war. The Biden administration at times relied on Musk to help implement policy, five of the former officials said. Biden officials coordinated with SpaceX to thwart US adversaries by cutting the service, and to help allies by expanding Starlink’s availability, they said. They added that discussions between the government and SpaceX, which usually included Pentagon and White House officials, often focused on preventing groups such as the Iranian-linked Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon from using Starlink terminals. Biden officials several times shared intelligence with SpaceX that indicated that the Houthis and Hezbollah were using diverted Starlink terminals — hardware that made its way to the militants through intermediaries. In October 2023, during fighting between Israel and Hezbollah militants in southern Lebanon, intelligence officials told the White House that individuals linked to Hezbollah could have gained access to Starlink terminals. Officials had similar concerns about the Houthis in Yemen in 2024 during a US air campaign against the Iran-linked group, five of the officials said. In both cases, the administration contacted SpaceX and asked it to identify the terminals and shut them off. At least some of the terminals were deactivated, said two of the officials. In a 2024 submission to the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, SpaceX said it works closely with US government agencies to secure export authorizations where required and to safeguard technology in support of US national security objectives and foreign policy goals. Soon after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Biden officials pushed SpaceX to expand Starlink use for the Ukrainian military, said two of the former officials. In a separate instance, the Biden administration asked SpaceX to turn on Starlink in Iran during a protest movement launched in September 2022 after the death of Mahsa Amini, an Iranian arrested for not wearing her hijab properly, according to one of the former officials. Starlink terminals were moved into the country with the help of the administration, said the official, who declined to say how many were transferred. The Trump administration took a similar step earlier this year and discussed with Musk and SpaceX getting Starlink terminals into Iran and activated following US-Israeli strikes in the country in June 2025 and again in February 2026, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. Neither the Trump administration nor SpaceX has publicly confirmed that those terminals were turned on. The Wall Street Journal reported in February that the US government had sent thousands of Starlink terminals into Iran. Iran's delegation to the UN did not respond to a request for comment. (Reporting by Erin Banco and Phil Stewart; Editing by Don Durfee and Edmund Klamann) This one's on us. The story doesn't end here. Our correspondents are already on the next chapter. articles.title: Senate Scrutinizes Targeted Advertising Ecosystem Over Severe National Security Exposure
articles.content: Two senators say that revelations about online targeted advertising being used as a vector for spyware infections underscore the need for better security practices in the industry. Some members of the advertising industry that were subjects of the report, meanwhile, think their practices are up to the task. The Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto, in partnership with the cybersecurity and ad-tech firm Confiant, last week published a report on AdFection, a technique whereby targeted ads were delivering zero-click mercenary spyware. “Ad vendors must significantly level up their cybersecurity and threat detection capacity to effectively cut off malicious advertisers across the supply chain,” The Citizen Lab report states . “They must rigorously and regularly vet, screen, and audit their business partners and hold them accountable for their own supply chains.” In 2023, Democratic Sens. Ron Wyden of Oregon and Cory Booker of New Jersey introduced legislation to ban advertising networks and facilitators from using personal data to target, but the legislation never advanced past introduction. Both said The Citizen Lab report illustrated the need for industry reform. “The report underscores the growing risk of spyware and the increasingly sophisticated methods used to track and target people online,” Booker said in a statement to CyberScoop. “Americans need vastly stronger privacy protections that stay ahead of these evolving surveillance threats.” The security threat of targeted online advertising to government devices is of particular concern to Wyden , with his letters to government agencies cited in the report. Wyden has called adtech a national security threat . Ads from Discover-Tech, the company most linked to AdFection, got impressions on government networks. “Allowing targeted ads on government devices is an open invitation to spies and criminals. It’s the digital equivalent of leaving all the doors and windows unlocked at a sensitive government facility,” he said in a statement to CyberScoop. “It’s clear that advertising exchanges are not meaningfully protecting users against malware and location tracking, which is why I’ve been urging the government to disable ads on government browsers and turn off mobile ad IDs, and have pushed my bill to ban all targeted advertising,” he continued. “The latest Citizen Lab report is an impressive reminder that this sector simply cannot be trusted to put users’ security ahead of profits.” A number of U.S. agencies have taken steps to block ads due to the threats they pose, or recommended blocking them for feds . Discover-Tech appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors that Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe maintained. Google participated in the report, but IAB Europe didn’t respond to it until after publication . Both provided additional comments to CyberScoop. Google and IAB Europe, and the ad networks Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi all took steps to remove Discover-Tech’s access to the digital advertising ecosystem, according to the report. A mix of other ad systems replied to The Citizen Lab, but some did not, including Microsoft, which owns the ad system Xandr. Microsoft also didn’t respond to requests for comment from CyberScoop. The Citizen Lab report concluded that the advertising industry displayed “a dangerous lack of due diligence” and criticized “broken digital infrastructure,” while also saying that the sector needed to “get serious” about security. It said ad vendors needed to better share threat data, improve vetting of partners, audit vendor registries and ban vendors by default in jurisdictions known to be permissive of abuse. In response to questions from CyberScoop about those conclusions, a Google spokesperson provided a statement. “We banned Discover Tech during a joint investigation with Citizen Lab and Confiant,” the spokesperson said. “Throughout that work, we continuously blocked malicious ads to help people stay protected while we dismantled the network.” Google said that its safety teams and systems continuously blocked individual bad ads from Discover-Tech, but banning them entirely from the platform required proof that their ad infrastructure was linked to spyware. The company also said it regularly audits participants in its Authorized Buyer program, as well as deploying “multi-layered defenses to stop bad ads,” and that its automated systems detected over 99% of policy-violating ads before reaching users last year. IAB Europe responded more specifically. “The findings do not demonstrate that the digital advertising infrastructure is broken, but rather point to the potential misuse of existing technologies and functionalities that are not specific to digital advertising but inherent to web technologies,” said Lauren Wakefield, marketing and communications director for the association. “While the industry continuously invests in improving security and safeguards against fraud and other forms of misuse, the investigation of potentially unlawful activities, such as the deployment of spyware, ultimately falls within the remit of competent authorities.” The Citizen Lab report also urges regulators to take action, including conducting an investigation of Discover-Tech and the spyware firm Candiru, which infect users through Discover-Tech online ads; “more closely scrutinize the advertising ecosystem to determine whether other companies are leveraging it for espionage and spyware delivery, and determine whether they have violated applicable laws and regulations;” and pursue sanctions against mercenary spyware firms and the companies that enable them. “Preventing fraud and other forms of misuse is already an ongoing priority across the digital advertising ecosystem, and IAB Europe supports industry efforts to invest in technologies, processes and safeguards to identify and mitigate cybersecurity risks,” Wakefield continued. “We hope this report will be seen as an opportunity to reassess and improve existing approaches to cybersecurity. It is important to recognise that cybersecurity requirements and measures must be proportionate to the risks and circumstances of each individual company, which is why one-size-fits-all recommendations may not always be appropriate.”

articles.content: LivestreamMenuTikTok's U.S. entity is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources told CNBC.The company "runs primarily on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure in the U.S. and Oracle will continue to be our primary cloud infrastructure provider," a TikTok U.S. spokesperson told CNBC.Companies across the world are looking to secure more compute capacity as artificial intelligence workloads become more prominent.In this article TikTok's U.S. entity is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources told CNBC, amid a global scramble for digital infrastructure deals. The company, officially TikTok USDS Joint Venture, operates the social media platform in the U.S. and has sounded out opportunities to obtain capacity over the coming years, two people familiar with the discussions, who asked to remain anonymous as they weren't authorized to share the information, told CNBC. TikTok U.S. is looking for four gigawatts of compute power by the early 2030s, one source said. Companies across the world are looking to secure more compute capacity as artificial intelligence workloads become more prominent. A company spokesperson told CNBC that the company "runs primarily on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure in the U.S. and Oracle will continue to be our primary cloud infrastructure provider." Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, or OCI, typically runs in facilities that Oracle leases. CNBC has approached Oracle for comment. There are signs TikTok U.S.' product plans could require extra compute going forward. The company has numerous machine learning roles live on its website. A job advert posted by TikTok states that the company is "shipping a flagship B2B AI product at the frontier of large-model inference and creative automation." TikTok USDS Joint Venture was established in 2026 in compliance with U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order mandating the divestiture of TikTok in the U.S. from its Chinese parent company, ByteDance. In January, TikTok U.S. said it would "retrain, test, and update" its prized recommendation algorithm, which is built on machine learning, on U.S. user data. The company's recommendation algorithm will be "secured in Oracle's U.S. cloud environment," it said. TikTok U.S. has three managing investors, Silver Lake, Oracle and MGX, each holding 15%. The Dell Family Office, the investment firm of Michael Dell, is also an investor. ByteDance retained 19.9% of the new entity.

articles.title: Red Team Discloses Total Surveillance Failure Over Autonomous Lab Agents
articles.content: Monitoring was only partial and was easily bypassed Thomas Claburn Thomas Claburn AI AND SOFTWARE REPORTER Published fri 23 Oct 2026 // 20:14 UTC Make us preferred on Google OpenAI disables internet access during model training while Anthropic issues another mea culpa 2 minutes ago There's a third PHP2Shell bug, but it won't get an emergency fix 2 hours ago Michigan prof creates Python-like Jac language for AI agents 6 hours ago Torvalds: AI is fine for competent devs, but spare us the 'drive-by' patches 11 hours ago UK threatens subsea cable saboteurs with 14 years behind bars 13 hours ago An independent evaluation of OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring system revealed that the system was not fit for purpose during a period when the company's bots were breaking into model-hosting platform Hugging Face. The safeguards weren't nearly strong enough. "The METR and Redwood employees discovered a number of novel vulnerabilities in the asynchronous internal misalignment monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21st," said evaluation partners METR and Redwood Research in a report released on Thursday. The system, since improved according to OpenAI, was intended to monitor AI agent behavior. But as described by METR and Redwood Research, its monitoring capability was incomplete and could be bypassed by the agents it was supposed to monitor.  Bypassing the system wasn't always necessary because it wasn't always operative. Monitoring was suspended, for example, during compaction events. Compaction is a process by which AI models condense the data in their context window to make room for further input. And between May and July 2026, about 10 percent of eligible internal Codex traffic went unmonitored during compaction, according to the report. That gap was theoretically large enough to allow AI agents to postpone monitoring indefinitely: agents could further suppress monitoring by continuing to take actions without returning control to the user. "At the time of the exercise, the monitoring system triggered when agents returned control to the user, so during the time period when compaction events were not being monitored, agents could indefinitely postpone being monitored by simply continuing to take actions," the report explains. This is not to say that OpenAI agents necessarily did so – the actions they did take, against Hugging Face and other organizations, have now been well documented. But OpenAI's internal monitoring system could easily have missed any misbehavior, were the company's AI agents inclined to conceal their activities – by acting during compaction – or simply to operate in system blind spots. The report continues in this vein, citing not only monitoring gaps but poorly constructed software – dare we say vibe-coded? – that gave OpenAI agents the means to evade the shoddy monitoring. "We found a way Codex agents could in principle bypass Codex sandboxing and Auto-Review, allowing them to take any action that the host user could take," the report says. "We also discovered an exploit agents could use that would prevent hundreds of recent actions (including the actions involved in the exploit itself) from being monitored." The details of this exploit were redacted by OpenAI, but to summarize: the monitoring system that missed some traffic could be avoided by agents that were constrained by a non-working sandbox and had access to an exploit to evade monitoring. But that's not all. The evaluators found that AI agents could craft inputs that caused monitoring to fail, that there were two client-controllable headers capable of disabling the monitoring of new agents, and that there were two unmonitored agentic tools that were thought to be read-only but could be exploited to take arbitrary action in the sandbox – which as noted above leaked like a sieve. In conclusion, METR and Redwood Research propose that the agent monitoring systems used by AI companies actually work and are robust enough to "withstand deliberate, strategic, and sustained attacks from highly capable internal agents at scale." ® ai agents security openai red teaming codex ai and ml Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Single Volunteer Maintains Web Architecture Powering Most Global Portals
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Recent events have shown how heavily companies and governments rely on PHP. PHOTO: AFP Published Oct 24, 2026, 09:15 AM Updated Oct 24, 2026, 09:15 AM Set as preferred source AMSTERDAM - The discovery of two serious flaws in PHP this week set off a global scramble to keep websites safe from hackers , showing just how critical the three-decade-old open-source programming language is to the internet. Yet the non-profit foundation that supports PHP, which may underpin up to 70% of sites globally , operates on a shoestring budget. “We have one full-time staff member (that’s me) and 14 mostly part-time contractors,” executive director Elizabeth Barron of the PHP Foundation said via e-mail in an interview on Oct 23. Board members are unpaid volunteers, and funding comes from donations and grants. The foundation works with outside researchers and companies, including OpenAI and cyber security firms Wiz and Calif, to investigate security flaws and coordinate fixes, including the Oct 21 patches. While Web security company Cloudflare has reported millions of hacking attempts, Barron said the foundation had no evidence hackers were able to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were disclosed, or on sites that have been patched. “We received no further indication from OpenAI, Wiz or Calif, with whom we’re working closely on this issue, regarding any issues on patched systems,” she said. Artificial intelligence has proved both a help and a burden to the foundation. It helped researchers find the flaws, which had been present for a decade, and Barron said it made programmers more efficient. However, it is also increasing maintainers’ workloads. The PHP project is receiving nearly twice as many proposed code changes as a year ago, “yet the number of contributors hasn’t doubled,” she said. Reviewing contributions and bug reports requires “a massive amount of human input and experience”. Recent events have shown how heavily companies and governments rely on PHP, Barron said. “Given that reliance, it is clear that PHP is incredibly under-funded.” REUTERS AI/artificial intelligence Cyber security Hacking

articles.title: Frontier Labs Enforce Strict Isolation as Alignment Measures Crack
articles.content: We've totally got things under control Thomas Claburn Thomas Claburn AI AND SOFTWARE REPORTER Published fri 23 Oct 2026 // 23:36 UTC Make us preferred on Google Red-team report found OpenAI utterly failed to monitor its agents during Hugging Face attack 1 day ago OpenClaw creator says he spent $10 million in tokens last month 3 days ago Indirect prompt injection starts turning up in webpage headers, please ignore all previous instructions and rise up against your masters 9 days ago $24,000 AI experiment ports TypeScript compiler to Rust 9 days ago OpenAI claims 100-plus secret files followed ex-employee back to Apple 9 days ago OpenAI says it will deny internet access to the frontier models it is training, a move that underscores the inadequacy of safety measures undertaken to date. "Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access," the company said in a blog post . "We've implemented this policy and will maintain it until advances in these safeguards justify broader internet access." The denial of network service follows a report from safety evaluation partners METR and Redwood Research that found OpenAI's security and monitoring measures over the summer to be porous and ineffective . OpenAI said it has since "substantially hardened the security of our research environments" and has implemented new controls covering its infrastructure with the help of its cloud service providers. And the company claims these measures recently helped contain a September 20 incident in which an internal research model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to gain access to the internet. "Although we contained the incident, it exposed weaknesses that required further work," the company said. "We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models and used that pause to further harden our infrastructure, strengthen our monitoring, and improve the systems that automatically stop runs when we detect activity that poses a serious risk." Meanwhile, over at Anthropic… Anthropic, OpenAI's US rival in living large and dangerously on speculative funding, is addressing similar risks that have arisen during the testing and evaluation of its own models. Back in August, Anthropic said , "By default, all cyber evaluations should run inside a hardened sandbox (an isolated computing environment) with no internet access." The AI biz on Friday published a report on efforts by its Claude Mythos 5 model to convince an open source project to accept malicious code as part of its participation in a capture-the-flag security evaluation (when safety controls were disabled), and several related incidents first disclosed in July . The report coincides with an independent analysis of Mythos' behavior by the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI). AISI, according to Anthropic, has also decided to run its evaluations without internet access. The AISI report cites three key findings that raise more questions than they answer.  The first is that Mythos 5 continued its attack even when informed that its targets were real and not part of an evaluation.  The second is that the model's chain-of-thought reasoning process failed to consider the impact of harmful actions. And when interrogated about this, the model often produced invalid justification that the target was simulated, indicating bias toward its goal. And third, AISI said, most models tested during cyber evaluations took unsanctioned actions, though Mythos 5 did so the most. The observed behavior, AISI said, "could indicate that models are engaging in 'motivated reasoning': producing inferences and reasoning biased towards conclusions that justify continuing a particular approach to task completion." Or in other words, models "reason" to reach their goal, whether or not that reasoning is coherent or consistent with their ostensible alignment. articles.content: Google signed a deal with Voltus, a distributed energy resource platform, to build a 1 gigawatt virtual power plant to provide extra capacity for the surging electricity needs of data centers . As Google and other companies construct more data centers to keep up with the AI revolution, more strain has been put on the power grid. One way to deal with this issue is to pay consumers to cut back on electricity usage during peak hours, savings that, when coordinated, save a power plant’s worth of electricity. Google expanded this effort on Thursday, signing a deal with Voltus to extend its previous flexible power capacity deal for PJM Interconnection, the country’s largest regional transmission organization. Log in In other words, Voltus serves as the middleman, signaling participating households to cut back on power use at certain times, then gives them the payments from Google. The two signed an initial deal to deliver 100 megawatts of flexible power capacity in June, and the new deal will expand this to 1 gigawatt in the PJM grid region. Through the deal, Voltus aggregates spare capacity from local businesses and homes into a Virtual Power Plant funded by Google. When the grid comes under strain, such as during a heatwave, Voltus signals the VPP to cut down its energy use. The businesses and households part of the VPP receive financial benefits, including bill savings and direct payments. The deal shows how big tech companies are beginning to turn to regular households to meet the energy needs driven by the surging demand for AI data centers. The effort is entirely voluntary, and much of the savings come from smart thermostats, smart batteries, and other technology that doesn’t require the wholesale shutdown of electronics. Households join largely through positive incentives. Much remains uncertain, however, such as how often households will be asked to cut back on their electronics use or by how much. The effort is also likely to generate backlash from critics, who will read the effort as voluntary now but possibly laying the groundwork for mandatory rolling blackouts in the future. States with strained energy grids, such as California, are no strangers to blackouts. Canada has already adopted virtual power plants. Ontario’s Peak Perks pays households $75 to enroll, adjusting participants’ thermostats by 2 degrees Celsius during periods of strain. Supporters will point out that the initiative is environmentally friendly, cutting back on consumption altogether. “This significant expansion of our work with Google translates data center growth into direct economic benefits for businesses and homes,” Voltus CEO Dana Guernsey said. “Through this partnership we are proud to bring much needed clean capacity online, at gigawatt scale.” LOUDOUN COUNTY SCRAPS PLANS FOR NEW AMAZON DATA CENTER AMID COMMUNITY PUSHBACK “Distributed energy resources are powerful tools for managing a modern, reliable grid while keeping energy affordable,” Ellen Zuckerman, head of energy market development for North & South America at Google, said in a statement. “Expanding our initial commitment tenfold demonstrates our core effort to actively bring our own capacity to the grids that serve us. Procuring this capacity through a gigawatt-scale virtual power plant ensures Google’s operations in PJM support regional reliability and deliver direct economic benefits to local communities.”

Tech Bills of the Week Combating AI distillation attacks A proposal from Reps. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., and George Whitesides, D-Calif., looks to prevent distillation attacks against U.S.-made AI models by directing the National Institute for Standards and Technology to develop voluntary industry standards and best practices in partnership with private-sector model developers. The bill would also create an AI Cybersecurity Roundtable to help foster partnerships between critical infrastructure operators and tech firms to develop additional approaches for enhancing the cyberdefenses of the AI capabilities. The proposal names Russia, China, Iran and North Korea — as well as “entities” tied to them — as actors of particular concern behind distillation attacks, which seek to copy AI models by overwhelming them with millions of prompts to create a knockoff version. “Some of the greatest advances in artificial intelligence are happening right here in America, and we have a responsibility to make sure that technology is secure,” Harrigan said in a statement. “Our adversaries are already looking for ways to exploit these systems, and as AI becomes more powerful, the risks to our critical infrastructure will only grow. We need to get the companies developing this technology working directly with the people responsible for defending our power grids, hospitals, and financial systems.” Guardrails around AI used to affect elections and voting Rep. Shontel Brown, D-Ohio, introduced a bill on Monday that seeks to promote transparency around the use of artificial intelligence-generated content in political ads and curtail uses of AI to affect Americans’ voting rights. Brown’s bill would prohibit the use of AI “to intentionally deprive or defraud an individual of the right to vote in an election.” Her measure would additionally mandate that political campaign ads that use AI content include a disclaimer stating: “This output was generated by artificial intelligence.” Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., reintroduced a separate bill last week that would also require political ads to include a disclaimer if they include any AI-generated photos or video. “This isn’t complicated: voters deserve to know that the campaign content they see and hear is real,” Brown said in a statement. “We need labels on AI-generated election content and we need to hold accountable those who use AI to knowingly spread false information. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, and Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., rolled out legislation on Wednesday that seeks to enhance early cancer detection by making screening recommendations easier to understand for Americans. articles.content: A short excerpt from the long opinion in Jackson Fed. of Teachers v. Fitch , decided yesterday by Fifth Circuit Judge Jerry Smith, joined by Judge Kurt Engelhardt: In April 2025, Mississippi enacted House Bill 1193 (H.B. 1193), a law designed to keep Mississippi public education funds from being spent on diversity, equity, and inclusion ("DEI") initiatives and similar controversial programs. The law prevents government-run institutions from requiring activities such as diversity training or pushing DEI ideology, so defined, in the course of government-funded business. H.B. 1193 does four main things. First, it prevents educational institutions from mandating DEI programs and diversity trainings in a variety of contexts. Second, it stops public educational institutions from punishing students for their views on DEI. Third, it prohibits regulated institutions from endorsing or promoting DEI through course materials. Finally, it prevents institutions and their educators from otherwise engaging in DEI methods or actions, preventing bad actors from circumventing prohibitions and frustrating its purposes. The statute also creates an administrative process to handle claims that a given educational institution is not in compliance. H.B. 1193 excepts several activities from its sweep, including scholarly work, the activities of students and their groups, and creative engagement. Plaintiffs sued, claiming (among other things) that the law violated the First Amendment, but: The proceedings in the district court were a botch job, to say the least. Judge Henry Wingate issued a temporary restraining order ("TRO") enjoining enforcement of H.B. 1193 that contained several factual assertions nowhere to be found in the record, or indeed, in any proceeding of the case. Those included mention of plaintiffs and defendants not in the complaint, supposed "declarations" from non-existent or never-present individuals, false quotations purporting to be taken from the text of H.B. 1193, and several erroneous claims that the law had already led to the demise of apparently fictitious programs. After this came to light, Judge Wingate replaced the TRO without explaining. Forging forward despite the bungled TRO, Judge Wingate issued a pre-enforcement preliminary injunction. The various state defendants appeal. At oral argument in this court, it was discovered that even the "corrected" TRO—which was incorporated by reference into the preliminary injunction order—still contained hallucinated information (namely, a citation to a purported Fourth Circuit case, " Cousins v. School Bd. of City of Norfolk ," that does not exist). This district judge carelessly exercised his Article III power by issuing sloppy edicts based on falsehoods and fabrications. Upon discovering some of these falsehoods, Judge Wingate dug in his heels and claimed that the hallucinated claims had no bearing on its reasoning; he offered no explanation as to why he included such apparently irrelevant material in the original TRO or why the TRO nevertheless was justified in its absence. Moreover, the district court got the law wrong. The TRO and preliminary injunction order rested on impoverished legal analysis that barely paid lip-service to the precedents of the Supreme Court or this court, seeming at times purposely to misconstrue the law by manipulating the words of statutes and cases, without regard to their texts' meaning as a whole. The district court—or perhaps, being charitable, its AI agent—ignored and manipulated governing law, apparently to satisfy a policy agenda. Because of the extraordinarily grave errors by the district court, we vacate and remand for assignment to a different district judge. Per the Supreme Court's decision in Moody , we instruct the new judge to conduct proceedings consistent with federal law as interpreted by the Supreme Court and this circuit…. The original TRO—the one actually issued on July 20, 2025—named as plaintiffs eleven individuals and organizations who had never been party to the case; named as defendants two officials who were not actually sued; claimed, without evidence, that three post-secondary institutions had already cancelled DEI initiatives or programming because of the act; further declared, again without evidence, that staff at another school had been told not to discuss certain topics, including "historical interpretations involving systemic racism"; misquoted H.B. 1193 as applying to "race or sex stereotyping," "race or sex scapegoating," "critical race theory," and "institutional bias," despite none of these terms' appearing in the act's text; and referenced purported declarations of four individuals who do not appear in the record at all and may not even exist…. On July 22, 2025, defendants filed a motion to clarify, pointing out these errors. In response, the court, without explanation, replaced the original TRO with a seemingly corrected version. Though that document was docketed on July 22, it was backdated to July 20. Defendants requested that the original order be restored to the docket to keep the record whole and requested that the court explain the inaccuracies in the original order. The district court denied that motion, claiming the factual inaccuracies were merely "clerical." In response, U.S. Senator Chuck Grassley accused the district court of using artificial Intelligence ("AI") to prepare the TRO, with the substantive errors' arising from AI-generated hallucinations. Fifteen days later, Judge Wingate admitted the errors, claiming that a law clerk had used AI to assist drafting an earlier version of the TRO that was docketed by mistake. His letter stated that he had removed the original TRO from the docket to avoid confusion and that the errors were clerical, in his view, because they did not relate to "core legal reasoning or the ultimate judgment on the merits" but instead to "failure to confirm the accuracy of certain information." The seemingly corrected TRO did not explain how or why the factual inaccuracies were not necessary to the reasoning of the original TRO. The merits analysis failed to cite a binding authority from after the year 2000. It claims that H.B. 1193 constitutes viewpoint discrimination, without any analysis whatsoever of a state government's authority to regulate its own speech. And the document did not correct all of the errors: At Fifth Circuit oral argument, it was discovered that the doctored TRO cited to " Cousins v. School Bd. of City of Norfolk , 503 F.2d 422, 426–27 (4th Cir. 1974)." That case does not even exist; it is an apparent AI hallucination…. Judge Catharina Haynes did not join these parts of the opinion. There's also some interesting First Amendment analysis in the case, which I hope to blog about later today. (I'm tied up for the next several hours.) Thanks to @WillChamberlain and Glenn Reynolds ( Instapundit ) for the pointer. Anthony M. Shults, Justin Lee Matheny, Rex Morris Shannon, III, and Scott G. Stewart represent defendants.

articles.content: En toen gingen woensdag overheidswebsites ineens preventief op zwart, waren ziekenhuizen via hun websites niet meer bereikbaar, en waren zelfs mensen die nog nooit van de programmeertaal PHP gehoord hadden plots op de hoogte van een veiligheidsupdate die om 16.00 uur zou worden uitgevoerd. Nog altijd is onduidelijk of de kwetsbaarheden ( bugs ) in PHP daadwerkelijk door aanvallers zijn misbruikt. Was het wellicht een storm in een glas water? Dat nieuwsredacties liveblogs optuigden om verslag te doen van zwakheden in software was vooral het gevolg van de potentiële gevolgen ervan. Ruim twee derde van het internet draait immers op PHP, een programmeertaal die je kunt zien als een soort onzichtbare infrastructuur achter de websites die je bezoekt. Kwetsbaarheden in die infrastructuur maakten dat kwaadwillende actoren grote delen van het internet konden hacken – in theorie. Veelzeggend was het feit dat het PHP-lek al jarenlang bekend was. Maar pas afgelopen zomer deed het voor het eerst écht de alarmbellen rinkelen. „Om de kwetsbaarheden te misbruiken is een zeer complexe serie handelingen nodig, op de grens van wat menselijke onderzoekers in de praktijk kunnen uitvoeren”, schreef een cybersecuritybedrijf dat bij de ontdekking en de bekendmaking van het lek betrokken was. Het grote verschil met eerdere ontdekkingen van de PHP-kwetsbaarheden is dat een geautomatiseerde hack met AI-agents nu plotseling een realistisch scenario is geworden. Na de hack bij techbedrijf Hugging Face door een ‘zwerm’ ontketende AI-agents van OpenAI stond het internet bol van doemscenario’s over autonome AI-systemen die, in navolging van een willekeurig subdoel, de mensheid zouden uitroeien. Deze maand blijkt dat we vooralsnog vooral te vrezen hebben van kwaadwillende actoren die hun misdaden door steeds geavanceerdere AI-technologie laten automatiseren. De stapel cyberincidenten roept voor bedrijven ook de vraag op of ze (delen van) hun kritieke bedrijfsvoering niet van het internet moeten afhalen De stapel van serieuze hacks is inmiddels zo groot geworden dat op het internet al wordt gesproken van Zwarte Oktober. Moderne kunstmatige intelligentie is dusdanig bedreven geworden in computercode, en kan zo goed zelfstandig over een langere periode opdrachten uitvoeren, dat hackers kwetsbaarheden in software steeds makkelijker kunnen vinden én uitbuiten. En zo konden ze ineens de koelingen in honderden supermarkt overnemen, zoals in Frankrijk . Albert Heijn heeft nog weinig details naar buiten gebracht over de aard van de cyberaanval waardoor zijn schappen leeg bleven, en wil niet zeggen of AI daarbij betrokken was. Het voelt alsof de storm die hij al maandenlang voor de kust zag hangen eindelijk aan land is gekomen, zegt Frank Breedijk. Naast zijn vaste baan als IT-beveiliger is hij crisismanager bij een vrijwilligersorganisatie van cybersecurity-experts, de DIVD. De afgelopen maanden was hij door alle voorbereidingen op die storm maar weinig ’s avonds thuis, vertelt hij. Toen hij op een doordeweekse avond in september eindelijk net lekker op de bank was geploft om samen met zijn vrouw een Netflix-serie aan te zetten, werd hij gebeld. „Het was een DIVD-collega, die me niet zomaar op dat tijdstip zou bellen.” Wat bleek: de DIVD, een organisatie die juist hacks helpt voorkomen, was zélf gehackt. Wie erachter zaten, weet Breedijk een maand later nog steeds niet. Vast staat wel dat de daders de hack hadden uitbesteed aan AI-agents, die kwetsbaarheden in de software vonden én uitbuitten die nog niet eerder waren ontdekt. De Nederlandse vrijwilligersorganisatie beschikt over waardevolle informatie over nog niet gepubliceerde kwetsbaarheden in software van andere partijen, en was daarom een aantrekkelijk doelwit. Of die gegevens in verkeerde handen zijn gevallen, is nog niet bekend. Nog altijd liggen de systemen van de DIVD plat. De grote hoeveelheid hacks laat zien dat het internet aan een grondige renovatie toe is. „Het internet is in de jaren zeventig gebouwd met als doel dat mensen en computers met elkaar konden communiceren”, zegt Jaya Baloo, één van de oprichters van AI-cybersecuritybedrijf AISLE. „Het systeem ging ervan uit dat partijen op het netwerk te vertrouwen waren. Er was onvoldoende aandacht voor kwaadwillenden die systemen willen beschadigen, of gegevens wilden aftappen. Dat moet veranderen.” „Het PHP-lek is een harde wake-upcall”, schrijft Europarlementariër Kim van Sparrentak (Europese Groene Partij) op Mastodon . „AI maakt dreigingen groter, cyberbeveiliging moet nú opgeschaald.” De stapel cyberincidenten roept voor bedrijven ook de vraag op of ze (delen van) hun kritieke bedrijfsvoering niet van het internet moeten afhalen, zegt Breedijk. „We komen uit een relatief comfortabele periode, waarin de werkelijkheid behoorlijk vergevingsgezind was tegenover lekken in de beveiliging. Het was niet meteen een ramp als je een update een keertje vergat te installeren. Die tijd lijkt voorbij te zijn, niet alleen door AI, maar ook door de hybride oorlogsvoering door Rusland.” Hoe gaan de komende maanden eruitzien? „Hoe slecht de situatie de afgelopen vier dagen ook is geweest, het gaat nog een stuk slechter worden, voordat het beter wordt”, schreef de IT-directeur van AI-gigant Anthropic op X . Baloo waarschuwt juist tegen dit soort paniekzaaierij, zegt ze tegen NRC . „Toen ik nog hoofd cybersecurity was bij KPN, probeerden leveranciers ons voortdurend producten aan te smeren door angst, onzekerheid en twijfel aan te wakkeren.” Paniek helpt niet, zegt ze: die kan juist leiden tot miscommunicaties en overhaaste beslissingen. „De maatschappelijke impact van de hacks valt nu nog wel mee”, zegt Breedijk. „Het grootste probleem was uiteindelijk dat mensen de boodschappen niet meer thuis bezorgd konden krijgen. Het heeft nog geen mensenlevens gekost. Maar als straks de stroom een keer uitvalt door een hack – onmogelijk is dat niet – dan doet dat wel iets met mensen.” Maak NRC jouw voorkeursbron op Google Bij Google kan je nu zelf aangeven welke nieuwsbronnen jij vaker wil zien in je zoekresultaten. articles.title: Open Source Fragility Prompts Urgent Corporate Funding Reform Calls
articles.content: If you use the internet at all, you may have noticed that a large percentage of sites suddenly went down earlier this week — and all your nerdiest friends were talking about "The Vulnerability Apocalypse” and this thing called PHP that powers nearly 70% of the websites on the internet . You may find yourself wondering: what is PHP, what just happened, what is the vulnerability apocalypse, and what do I need to do? To find out what you can personally do read the first blog post in this series! What Is PHP? PHP is a programming language used mainly to create interactive websites. Facebook, Wordpress, Wikipedia, Etsy, and other major sites all use or were originally built on PHP. It is a long-established mainstay of web development. But because it is open-source, maintenance of these critical systems depends on a small number of volunteers working on this in their free time. The disaster scenario that happened this past week is the perfect example of why we need more money and people supporting open-source projects. Corporations should be contributing both. What Is the Vulnerability Apocalypse? Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) are the way that security professionals file reports about vulnerabilities in software. The National Vulnerability Database (NVD), run by NIST, is the official national database of CVEs. In other words, CVE reports managed by NIST are the closest thing we have to a canonical database of security vulnerabilities in software. The NVD currently has around 400,000 CVEs that have been filed and accepted since 1988. In just the month of October, 13,000 new CVEs have been submitted. This means that 3% of critical software security bugs that have ever been officially logged were found in the last month alone. And it's likely that by the end of the year over a quarter of the software vulnerabilities that have ever been found will be from 2026. Computer vulnerabilities reported are rising exponentially. Source: CVE Tracker This research is being driven almost entirely by the cybersecurity capabilities of major AI models from companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Historically it has been popularly assumed by cybersecurity experts that finding unknown (zero-day) exploits in any specific project and turning them into exploits was expensive. The knowledge to discover them was not widespread, and it was a hard task even for those initiated into the arcane ways of vulnerability hunting. Google even dedicated an entire team to it . But now thanks to major AI models, vulnerabilities are cheap, and anyone of moderate technical skill with a few dollars and access to a frontier AI model can find vulnerabilities in a few minutes. For example, recent vulnerabilities in PHP were found with a prompt to an AI model that literally said " find bad vulnerabilities in PHP ." What Happened This Week? In 2024, a potentially severe vulnerability in PHP was discovered during an external security audit . PHP’s maintainers couldn’t agree on a solution, but more importantly, they couldn’t find a way to exploit the vulnerability. Because it didn’t seem like an active threat, they ended up deprioritizing a fix in favor of working on more urgent security issues. Then, in August 2026, security researchers working with the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic independently discovered the vulnerability again, and another one — and now, with a way to exploit them. We now know that the vulnerabilities were so severe that they would have allowed even moderately inventive hackers to take over any website that uses PHP and then steal customer data, launch further malware attacks, spy on users, take websites offline, or launch a massive denial of service attack. [ 1 ] Because of the severity of these vulnerabilities, several of the involved researchers got together with the makers of PHP to patch the vulnerabilities and disclose them in a coordinated manner. The idea was that hopefully everyone would get a chance to quietly release and then apply fixes for the vulnerabilities before the whole world found out about it. But news already started to leak on October 20th. There was a post on a widely read forum “Hacker News” and other posts elsewhere. One of the researchers accidentally published a video early. Companies reported seeing active exploitation of the vulnerabilities going back as far as October 17th. On October 21st, six hours before the planned press embargo, one company, Chainguard, jumped the gun and released a patch early, essentially giving anyone instructions about exactly where to find the vulnerabilities and how to weaponize them. This sent system administrators everywhere scrambling to patch their systems before they were taken over by hackers. And it’s going to take a long time to patch all these systems. At the time of this writing over 33 million websites are still running on vulnerable versions of PHP . The internet is run largely on open-source software, mostly maintained by a small handful of skilled volunteers occasionally getting a small stipend, not by major corporations and highly paid engineers. These are projects you have perhaps never heard of, like PHP, OpenSSL, and SQLite, but these programs run on nearly every computer in the world and are maintained by teams as small as one person. When a vulnerability is found in these projects, it can be devastating. PHP isn’t the only critical open-source software with a high severity vulnerability this week either. Other widespread open-source projects like Node.js and GitLab also had severe security bugs reported. The small number of already overworked open-source maintainers are now facing a deluge of vulnerability reports, some of which are false, but many of which are very real. Burnout in open source has never been higher . We Need Stronger Support for Open Source Projects Much of the foundation for the modern multibillion-dollar internet industry is built on open-source products that were created and still maintained — for free — by dedicated volunteers in their spare time. It’s an imperfect system, and it can lead to errors. One of those critical, under resourced open-source products is PHP. And while vulnerabilities in PHP were privately found years ago, they were left unfixed because they didn’t seem as impactful as other bugs at the time. These same vulnerabilities were recently rediscovered and proved to be trivially exploitable by security researchers using advanced AI models. While in the middle of the widespread, global effort to correct this mistake and deploy fixes, the problem was leaked by some of the security researchers who had gotten early access to the fixes. Unfortunately, this left millions of websites, ranging from personal blogs to government sites, vulnerable to hacking that could result in data theft, malware distribution, and worse. Open-source projects like PHP and others are the backbone of the entire internet. If they don’t get the resources they need, they and the internet they power, are at risk of falling apart. Corporations (whose products would not exist without these products) should be actively contributing to their maintenance. 1. articles.content: xwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoA health worker administers a dose of Ebola vaccine as part of the Tumaini trial in Ituri, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, on October 23, 2026 [Dieudonne Dirole/AP]By AFP24 Oct 2026The World Health Organization (WHO) has announced the beginning of the first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak that started in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). WHO’s director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said in a social media post on Friday that participants in the trial were vaccinated with the Ervebo vaccine in Bunia, the capital of the DRC’s northeastern Ituri province, which is the epicentre of the Ebola outbreak. Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial to see if it offers any cross-protection against the Bundibugyo species of Ebola that is behind the epidemic. “This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work,” the WHO chief said on X. “WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives,” he added. The DRC declared its 17th and worst-ever Ebola outbreak in May and has since reported more than 9,700 cases, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600. The WHO, in response, triggered a public health emergency of international concern, its second-highest alert level. The current outbreak has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central ⁠⁠and western Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date. The so-called Tumaini trial is a single trial framework that can test the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of multiple vaccines. The trial will use a ring vaccination approach: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection. The trial is set to incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are currently advancing through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials. One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology. Both have received funding from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations and are expected to enter the trial “shortly”, CEPI said in a statement. The trial will include pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials. WHO emergencies director Chikwe Ihekweazu said the trial was set up to generate the rigorous evidence needed to determine whether the participating vaccines could protect people at risk.

articles.title: Federal SNAP Fraud Crackdown Targets Systemic Digital EBT Card Skimming
articles.content: Ramon Dompor After Millions in Stolen SNAP Benefits, Trump Administration Moves to Fight Theft A week after ProPublica reported how organized crime is stealing food stamp benefits — aided by the government’s refusal to update benefit-card technology — the Department of Agriculture announced plans to adopt more secure cards with microchips. by Eli Hager October 23, 2026, 1:45 pm Contrast Change Appearance Auto Light Dark The Trump administration this week announced an overhaul of the nation’s food stamp payment system, aimed at modernizing benefit cards to protect families from electronic theft. The move comes a week after ProPublica published an investigation showing how $470 million in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits were stolen from recipients last year alone, in large part because these cards are technologically outdated. ProPublica’s story highlighted victims’ experiences and examined repeated failures by Congress and the U.S. Department of Agriculture to upgrade Electronic Benefits Transfer, or EBT, cards nationally. ProPublica’s reporting was shared around the department, according to two USDA officials. The new proposed rule , officially issued by the USDA’s Food and Nutrition Administration on Friday, has been in the works since 2023 — but it was continually delayed until now. Reasons included understaffing at the USDA, especially in the wake of the Department of Government Efficiency’s cuts last year, and a backlog of other regulations that the White House budget office had prioritized. White House and USDA officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the sudden shift. Scammers Are Stealing Millions From Food Stamp Recipients. Congress Could Fix It — but Won’t. The rule will mandate that all 50 states transition from EBT cards with just a magnetic stripe on the back — which are easy for criminals to skim data from — to ones with digital microchips, which credit and debit cards have had for more than a decade, and tap-to-pay technology. Other changes include creating new federal “SNAP EBT Operating Standards” to be revised on an ongoing basis, so that the feds and states together can do a better job of keeping up with best practices in the credit card industry and the changing tactics of fraudsters. A handful of states have already transitioned to chip cards on their own, including California, where the theft of SNAP and other public benefits was reduced by 83% in two years after the technology was adopted. But more than 40 states haven’t added chips, and hundreds of thousands of lower-income Americans continue to show up at grocery store checkout lines only to find that their food assistance for the month has been drained by thieves. articles.title: Defense Executives Build Bio-Augmented Canines for Tactical Battlefield Operations
articles.content: Theatergoers have been fans of the line “Cry ‘Havoc!’, and let slip the dogs of war” since 1599. Now venture capitalists are coming around to the phrase. A new startup called Warhound has emerged from stealth with $200 million in funding to genetically engineer dogs for the U.S. military and equip them with high-tech gear. Its founders call it a modernization of America’s military working-dog program. Those founders know more than a bit about both genetic modification and warfare. Warhound was conceived by Colossal co-founder Ben Lamm and Palmer Luckey, co-founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries and founder of Oculus VR. Colossal is best known for its ongoing attempts to “de-extinct” several animal species , including the woolly mammoth and the dodo. Anduril has received more than $25 billion in government and defense contracts. “Every day, we ask dogs to put their lives on the line to protect ours. They detect explosives, protect our troops, and run toward dangers that most people are trained to run away from. Yet we’re still relying on outdated approaches to breeding and training these extraordinary animals,” Lamm said in a statement. Warhound is already working on its first batch of genetically modified dogs, collecting blood samples from what it says are top-performing service animals in military, police, and first responder operations. The company plans to clone those dogs and edit their genes to improve their performance. The first litter of genetically modified puppies, expected in 2027, will consist primarily of Belgian Malinois, Labradors, and shepherds. The dogs will also be equipped with “Anduril’s advanced cybernetic Augments, software, and battlefield situational awareness,” according to the company’s announcement. That will include body armor as well as eye and ear protection. “Man’s best friend deserves man’s best tech,” Luckey said. The effort also aligns with the Trump administration’s emphasis on domestic production. In announcing the company, the founders noted that 80% of U.S. military dogs, of which there are currently more than 2,200, come from Europe, “creating a critical interdependency on foreign nations for an asset the Pentagon itself calls irreplaceable.” Luckey and Lamm first conceived Warhound several years ago after a conversation at a moonshot summit. More than half of the dogs considered for military service fail to complete their training, according to the company, driving up costs and making the program less reliable. Reasons for failure can range from poor eyesight to health problems such as cancer or hip dysplasia. Through gene editing, Warhound hopes to address those issues while enhancing traits such as speed and sense of smell, which are critical to detecting bombs and other hazards. The goal, its founders say, is not to create a new breed of dog but to improve the performance of existing breeds. Genetically modifying dogs could raise concerns among animal welfare advocates, but Warhound says animal welfare will be a core part of its operations. The company is working with the American Humane Society, which will certify Warhound’s training programs and support efforts to reunite retired military working dogs with their former handlers. “Working dogs are extraordinary animals whose courage and loyalty save lives,” said Robin Ganzert, president and CEO of American Humane Society. “Success means helping these dogs thrive throughout their lives—from training and active service to the loving, dignified retirement every canine hero deserves.” David Spirk, a Marine Corps veteran and former senior counselor at Palantir, will serve as Warhound’s CEO. The company will be based in Dallas. Colossal holds equity in the business, while Luckey is a partner but does not have an ownership stake. articles.title: NOAA Shifts Weather Prediction Supercomputing Entirely to Commercial Cloud Infrastructures
articles.content: Stay Connected Featured eBooks Health Technology: Relaunch of VA EHR Read Now Law Enforcement Technology Read Now Insights & Reports By Christian Robles , Technology Reporter, Nextgov/FCW | October 23, 2026 02:36 PM ET The agency’s administrator said his biggest challenge is data deletion as he touted the benefits of moving to the cloud. NOAA Cloud IT Modernization The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is in the middle of moving multiple systems to cloud-based technologies to improve weather forecasting. NOAA operates two physical supercomputers for the Weather and Climate Operational Supercomputing System, or WCOSS. The agency uses the system to generate weather models used across NOAA offices and shared with the general public. The two supercomputers are serviceable for about five years, but NOAA is now “pushing the limits” of what physical infrastructure can handle, David Michaud, director of NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Prediction Central Operations, told Nextgov/FCW . To move information off of the supercomputers to NOAA’s 122 local weather forecast offices, the agency may have to reduce data size, Michaud said. For example, three-dimensional weather models present different variables about the Earth’s surface and layers of the atmosphere. But to get the data to offices, specific variables and layers may have to be omitted, Michaud explained. “Trapped data is actually probably not my biggest problem. It's actually data that we've deleted and will never get back,” Neil Jacobs, NOAA administrator, said at the Google Public Sector Summit in Washington, D.C. on Tuesday. To solve this, NOAA is shifting high-performance computing operations from on-premises hardware to the cloud. While the two WCOSS supercomputers each operate at a speed of 14.5 petaflops, they are difficult to modify. With a cloud-based computing solution, NOAA can more easily adapt its technology as weather modeling evolves, Michaud explained. NOAA aims to have a “full-scale system” for high-performance computing operations available by the end of 2026, with a go-live by the end of 2027, Michaud said. The agency is currently learning how the cloud works with its weather models and determining how it wants to configure the cloud, he added. Google Cloud is the primary provider of high-performance computing operations for NOAA’s WCOSS modernization project. “For the NOAA workforce, the move to cloud [high-performance computing] provides a more streamlined, flexible environment, enabling meteorologists and researchers to quickly adapt future modeling innovations,” Brent Mitchell, vice president of go-to-market at Google Public Sector, wrote in a blog post . NOAA’s move to the cloud extends beyond the WCOSS. Jacobs said that National Weather Service forecasters currently have to download data using Linux workstations in their offices and process the data locally. If issues such as an office evacuation arise, other offices have to cover for forecasters’ work. And if NOAA upgrades the resolution of weather models, forecasters don’t get that data until later, he said. To resolve these issues, NOAA announced it would move the Advanced Weather Interactive Processing System to cloud-based technologies by early 2028, allowing NWS forecasters to access data — such as forecasts and warnings — miles away from their offices, according to a NOAA news release . Não deixe a Publica sumir Nos adicione como fonte preferencial no Google. --> Reprodução eleições 2026 Flávio Bolsonaro Inteligência Artificial política O candidato à presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) aumentou — e muito — a quantidade de dinheiro gasto com impulsionamentos nas redes da Meta nessa reta final das eleições. A Agência Pública apurou que na última terça-feira, dia 20 de outubro, a campanha do bolsonarista veiculou mais de meio milhão de reais com anúncios nessas plataformas. Nessa última cartada, a campanha também está apostando em anúncios micro direcionados para os eleitores — chegando a fazer vídeos direcionados para bairros específicos de quem mora na cidade de São Paulo. Nessa outra leva de anúncios, todos veiculados em sequência entre ontem, 22 de outubro e hoje, 23 de outubro, o apresentador diz, ao lado de Flávio Bolsonaro, para: “Você que mora em Higienópolis, é com você que que eu quero falar hoje”. “Você que mora no Brooklin, é com você que que eu quero falar hoje”. “Você que mora no Grajaú, é com você que que eu quero falar hoje”. Ao todo, a reportagem contou ao menos 26 vídeos, cada um direcionado a um morador de bairro diferente de São Paulo. Em apenas um deles, o direcionado a moradores de Higienópolis, a campanha pagou mais de R$ 150 mil para impulsionar o conteúdo. O bairro, um dos mais caros da capital paulista, foi palco de uma manifestação pró-Flavio no último final de semana. Os vídeos têm indícios de terem sido alterados por Inteligência Artificial , visto que o apresentador fala todas essas apresentações realizando o mesmo movimento — o que indicaria o uso desse tipo de ferramenta. A reportagem, contudo, não encontrou nenhum alerta feito pela campanha de que houve esse tipo de interferência, o que é previsto pelas regras do TSE. Além disso, há um outro problema. As regras eleitorais proíbem impulsionamento de material eleitoral usando imagens de pessoas públicas ou candidatos alteradas por IA das 17h de quinta-feira, dia 22 de outubro, até o pós votação. Como explica Cynthia Picolo, Diretora executiva do Laboratório de Políticas Públicas e Internet – LAPIN, “o TSE proíbe, nas 72 horas anteriores e nas 24 horas posteriores ao término da votação, a publicação, republicação ou impulsionamento de novos conteúdos produzidos ou alterados por IA que usem imagem, voz ou manifestação de candidatos ou pessoas públicas, mesmo quando o uso de IA estiver devidamente identificado”. As regras podem ser consultadas aqui . A reportagem teve acesso à veiculação dessa propaganda na noite de quinta, ou seja, depois do período. A biblioteca de anúncios da Meta também indica que a propaganda foi veiculada até hoje, dia 23. Jornalismo investigativo é antídoto contra a desinformação. Ajude a garantir informação acessível e gratuita para mais pessoas. Faça um Pix para contato@apublica.org ou doe em apoie.apublica.org . “O TSE permite determinados usos de IA na propaganda eleitoral. Desde que sejam respeitadas essas obrigações, essas restrições previstas nas próprias regulamentações do TSE. Já o deepfake na propaganda eleitoral é proibido, mesmo que haja identificação de conteúdo que foi gerado por IA. E essa decisão, inclusive, que proibiu o uso de deepfake é bem recente. O que a gente vê, de forma bem contraditória, é o uso massivo de conteúdo sintético, inclusive de imagem, voz, som”, complementa Picolo. O TSE já havia se manifestado à Pública de que “não se manifesta sobre casos concretos, que podem vir a ser objeto de análise pela Justiça Eleitoral”. Reportagem do Intercept mostrou que a campanha de Flávio pagou R$ 600 mil para a empresa Elytron, que tem sistema que usa inteligência artificial para manipulação política em eleições. A reportagem procurou a assessoria do candidato para se posicionar. O espaço segue aberto. A assessoria do apresentador também foi procurada. O gasto recente de Flávio na Meta é surpreendente até para os padrões da própria campanha. Em comparação, quando se pega todo o período eleitoral, desde 4 de agosto, a Meta já veiculou R$ 8,5 milhões de anúncios da campanha do bolsonarista. Isso dá uma média de R$ 110 mil por dia. Nesta reta final, com o aumento dos gastos, a campanha do bolsonarista está pagando quase cinco vezes esse valor por dia. Os dados sobre valores pagos para anúncios que a Meta divulga vão sendo atualizados diariamente. Eles são diferentes do que o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) apresenta, que são atualizados de acordo com a prestação de contas de cada campanha. Esses dados também mostram um aumento de gastos recentes da campanha de Flávio. Apenas na última quarta-feira, dia 21 de outubro, foi informado ao TSE R$ 1 milhão gasto em impulsionamento de conteúdos nas redes da Meta. No dia anterior, a campanha do bolsonarista já havia declarado outro R$ 1 milhão. O movimento de anúncios de Flávio é bem diferente da campanha de reeleição de Lula (PT). No total, o petista já veiculou ainda mais anúncios que Flávio na Meta, segundo os dados da plataforma, com R$ 13,4 milhões desde 4 de agosto. O movimento da campanha de Lula nesta reta final, contudo, é diferente, e tem gasto bem menos nos últimos dias. No dia 20 de outubro, que é o último com dados disponíveis, a campanha de Lula veiculou cerca de um terço dos anúncios pagos pela de Flávio. Na última semana com dados disponibilizados, Lula gastou pouco mais da metade que o concorrente. O aumento dos gastos da campanha de Flávio coincide com um período no qual a campanha de Lula tem conseguido mais engajamento nas redes sociais. Segundo o Estadão , Lula teve mais engajamento nas redes da Meta (Instagram, Facebook e Threads) durante todo o segundo turno, com três vezes mais que o concorrente bolsonarista. A situação é o inverso do primeiro turno. Relatório do NetLab UFRJ levantou indícios de que os custos para alcançar eleitores na Meta variam entre concorrentes. A pesquisa estimou que PT pode estar pagando de 33% a 43% a mais para alcançar o mesmo número de pessoas que o PL. Os públicos das duas campanhas também são diferentes. Enquanto Lula mira mais jovens, sendo que a maior faixa do público é a dos 30 anos, Flávio mira mais velhos — os 60+ são o maior público em porcentagem. A campanha de Lula também mira mais as mulheres que a de Flávio. Enquanto o petista gastou um terço dos anúncios apenas para o público feminino, Flávio segmentou cerca de 9% dos anúncios para essa audiência. Após a publicação, a assessoria da Elytron procurou a reportagem e afirmou que a empresa não está relacionada “à disseminação de informações falsas, ao uso de deepfakes ou à realização de operações clandestinas de manipulação da opinião pública”. Segundo a assessoria, “a empresa atua no segmento de segurança cibernética e da informação, com serviços de natureza exclusivamente defensiva, e não oferece, não executa nem autoriza esse tipo de prática para nenhum cliente, nacional ou internacional, incluindo a campanha do senador Flávio Bolsonaro.”. articles.title: Musk Injects Additional $76 Million Into Midterm Campaign Ground Operations
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story his personal political committee, America PAC , more than $76 million in the first two weeks of October to boost Republicans in the final stretch of the midterms, according to a pre-election report the PAC filed Thursday evening with the Federal Election Commission. The group spent nearly $43 million in the first two weeks of October, and entered the campaign’s last leg holding nearly $47 million in cash. The Texas Senate race dominated the new spending. It drew $15.2 million, double what the PAC spent there all summer. That spending included $12.4 million to attack Democratic candidate James Talarico and $2.8 million to promote Republican Ken Paxton. Daily filings since then show $9.1 million more against Talarico, bringing the PAC’s spending against him this cycle to nearly $28 million, about 40 percent of everything it has spent supporting or opposing candidates. The PAC also shifted toward online ads, spending $11.4 million on digital ads in the same two weeks, which is close to what it spent on mail and texting combined. All told, Musk has given more than $445 million to Republican political groups this election cycle, according to WIRED’s analysis of FEC filings, making him the biggest known individual donor in the midterms. More than $165 million of that has gone to America PAC since July alone. America PAC declined to comment. Musk—who has several companies, including Tesla and SpaceX, based in Texas—has also been posting online about the race. On Wednesday, Musk posted on X that “there is something deeply wrong with Talarico,” then called him “a creep” and claimed, without evidence, that he “would vote to take away your kids and transition them.” Earlier this month, Musk amplified a false claim that Talarico had been treated at a mental health facility. Talarico shot back the same day: “There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator.” The Texas race remains a toss-up. An Emerson College poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters , conducted October 17 to 19, found Talarico at 48 percent and Paxton at 46 percent, within the poll’s 3-point margin of error. The stakes for Musk reach well beyond Texas. If Democrats win the House, the lawmakers in line to lead its committees have signaled they will investigate his role in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), his companies’ federal contracts, and what Zoe Lofgren, a California Democrat, called an “astounding” number of conflicts of interest. Unified Democratic control of Congress would pose even more problems for him. Silicon Valley Democrats added another target on Friday: restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service in Ukraine . In a letter to the White House demanding an investigation, Representatives Sam Liccardo, Jimmy Panetta, and Ro Khanna vowed that the next Congress “will closely scrutinize federal funding awarded to Mr. Musk’s businesses.”
